one_liner: Header-only C++20 fixed-capacity bump arena with frame rollback; about 1.2-1.8x faster per allocate() than std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource.
what_it_does: ArenaPro::Arena<EnableStats> owns one aligned buffer allocated once in the constructor and hands out memory by bumping an offset; allocate(size, align) returns nullptr (noexcept) when full instead of growing. It adds typed allocate<T>(), create<T>(args...) for in-place construction, destroy() that only runs the destructor, up to 8 nested beginFrame()/endFrame() checkpoints with an RAII ArenaScope, and O(1) reset(). It is its own interface, not a std::pmr::memory_resource or a std allocator, so it does not plug into pmr containers.
how_it_is_fast: Classic bump-pointer (linear/monotonic) allocation: alignment is rounded with a power-of-two mask derived from countr_zero, followed by two independent bounds checks, so the hot path is a few integer ops on one cache line. There is no upstream resource, no virtual dispatch (unlike std::pmr::memory_resource::allocate) and no block chaining, which is where its edge over monotonic_buffer_resource comes from. Optional statistics compile away via if constexpr and [[no_unique_address]].
when_to_use: Per-frame or per-request scratch memory with a known upper bound, reclaimed all at once with reset() or a scoped frame.
Hot loops doing many small, short-lived allocations (a few to a few hundred bytes) where a virtual call into std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource shows up.
Code that must treat out-of-memory as a plain nullptr branch with no exceptions (games, embedded-ish, real-time paths).
Over-aligned blocks (cache-line or page aligned) carved from one buffer, provided the arena is constructed with that base alignment.
when_not_to_use: Unknown or unbounded memory needs: capacity is fixed at construction and there is no growth or chaining.
Workloads that need per-object free or reuse of freed holes; destroy() never returns storage.
When you need std::pmr containers or an allocator-aware interface; it is not a memory_resource, so std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource over a fixed buffer is the drop-in choice.
Many short-lived arenas: construction is about 7x slower than monotonic_buffer_resource (23.4 ns vs 3.3 ns in the committed Google Benchmark run) because the buffer is allocated eagerly.
Shared use across threads: no synchronization is documented or present.

integration.dependencies: none (CMake 3.20+ for the install/find_package path; Google Benchmark only for the benchmark suite)
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (concepts, <bit>, [[no_unique_address]]); README lists GCC, Clang, MSVC and AppleClang as tested
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the class has no locking or atomics, so treat one arena as single-threaded
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same bump-allocation model as std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource, but a different, non-virtual API that returns nullptr instead of growing or throwing

gotchas: Preconditions are assert()-only (AP_PRE expands to assert): with NDEBUG, a ninth nested beginFrame() writes past the 8-slot frame stack, endFrame() without a matching beginFrame() underflows frameDepth_, and a request alignment above the construction alignment is silently not honored.

Reset + refill and failure-path speedups (hundreds to hundreds of thousands of percent) are not like-for-like: the benchmark calls monotonic_buffer_resource::release(), which returns its 64 MiB upstream block so the refill re-allocates it every iteration, and the bounded std side signals exhaustion by throwing std::bad_alloc that the loop catches.

The README describes the baseline as 'a naive new[] + linear-scan stdArena', but benchmarks/{custom,google}/support/reference.h define stdArena as std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource; and the README table's numbers match neither committed baseline (v1.0.0.md or gv1.0.0.md).
Several committed Google Benchmark rows (destroy_*, reset_arena, reset_std) report 0.00 ns, i.e. the work was optimized away; ignore them.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over NotKeira/fast-alloc or cleeus/obstack when you want a single bounded buffer with nested RAII rollback, nullptr-on-full semantics, and a fuzzed, sanitizer-tested C++20 header; pick fast-alloc for pool (fixed-size free list) needs and a general malloc replacement such as mimalloc-class siblings for anything unbounded.
verified_claims_summary: The committed comparisons are against std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource (not new[] as the README says): in the Google Benchmark v1.9.1 run on a 4-CPU GitHub Actions runner (clang Release, CPU model not recorded) allocate() costs 0.73 vs 1.31 ns small, 0.77 vs 1.07 ns for 256 B and 0.73 vs 1.07 ns at 64 B alignment (about 1.4-1.8x, derived from page data), while the custom-framework 1M-iteration run shows 0.62 vs 1.34 ms small. The headline reset+refill (64.7 ns vs 43.8 us) and failure-path (0.12 vs 907 ns) gaps come from release() freeing the upstream block and from exception handling, and construction is about 7x slower.
status_note: Active (v1.0.0 released 2026-07-28, commits into October 2026, 1 star, no issues filed); MIT, small and header-only, so easy to vendor, with CI for sanitizers, clang-tidy, CodeQL and ClusterFuzzLite differential fuzzing.
